findings.text: Within the first paragraph, a newcomer can say what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. The page meets the 'what is it' and 'why it matters' tests early.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: This is Athena's homepage, but the title and nearly all of the content are about a different project, firstmate. Athena's main feature (turning a request into a traced commit with cost and verdict) is described but never shown, so a newcomer must work out for themselves how a study relates to that feature.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The next step is clear and concrete: prerequisites, clone, `./setup.sh` and a one-line example command. The page links to it from the header ("Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself"), so a newcomer does not need to scroll through the study to find it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The prerequisites name only Claude Code, so a newcomer cannot tell where the second checking model comes from. The page also does not say whether an account or API cost is needed before trying it.
findings.source: Header lede: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it" vs Next steps: "either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)"

findings.text: This link is aimed at the project owner, but it sits in the header that newcomers read first. A first-time visitor has no decisions waiting and gets no explanation of what this link is.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The state list shows only a name, a tag and claim ids. A reader who comes straight here has to find each state's meaning in the leadin or the Glossary.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "queued initial [c1] [c2] [c43]"

findings.text: Some transition cards pack many edge cases and undefined terms ("pin", "endpoint") into one summary. That makes the firstmate study hard going for a newcomer, though the Glossary helps with some terms.
findings.source: t8 card summary: "A ship or scout keeps its recorded harness and needs a note; a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead."

findings.text: The page says plainly that nothing was run and that the claims come only from reading the code. A reader can trust its limits, and this supports the page's message about accountability.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"

findings.text: This section only makes sense to someone who already has the Athena repository. A newcomer gets nothing from it.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
